# Data Collection

## Purpose

The purpose of the data collection stage is to assemble a documented
longitudinal evidence base for analysing Australian national research
computing demand and allocation.

The project draws primarily on publicly available NCMAS outcomes and
NCI and Pawsey reporting to identify historical requested compute,
allocated compute, resource type, Field of Research and other available
characteristics of national HPC allocations and usage
[@HPCInternshipBrief].

Additional datasets, including research funding, workforce and research
activity indicators, are collected as potential structural drivers of
future HPC demand where sufficiently consistent time-series data are
available [@HPCInternshipBrief].

Because the availability, scope and definition of variables differ
substantially across years and sources, the purpose of this stage is not
to assume that all collected observations are directly comparable.
Instead, original values, units, reporting periods, source definitions
and data limitations are retained so that their suitability for
integration, standardisation and modelling can be assessed in subsequent
stages.

## Data Sources

The project uses multiple public data sources from NCI, Pawsey and
NCMAS, together with research funding, workforce and Field of Research
datasets.

The specific HPC source varies by analytical year. Earlier observations
are primarily drawn from annual reports, allocation documents and other
historical NCI and Pawsey publications, while more recent observations
increasingly use direct NCMAS outcome pages, applicant guidance and
facility-specific allocation information.

In several years, different documents are used for different analytical
components. Allocation outcomes, requested-demand information, resource
availability and Field of Research composition may therefore originate
from separate official publications.

For transparency and reproducibility, the exact source document,
source location and URL are retained in the underlying yearly datasets.
The principal sources used for each analytical year are summarised below.

Key source families include NCI annual and allocation reports
[@NCI201314; @NCI201415; @NCI201516; @NCI201617; @NCI201718;
@NCI201819; @NCI201920; @NCIAllocations201920;
@NCIAllocations202021], Pawsey annual and allocation publications
[@Pawsey201415; @Pawsey201617; @Pawsey2019NCMAS], and NCMAS
outcomes and applicant guidance [@NCMAS2014Info; @NCMAS2018Results;
@NCMAS2020Info; @NCMAS2021; @NCMAS2022; @NCMAS2023Info;
@NCMAS2023; @NCMAS2024; @NCMAS2024Info; @NCMAS2025;
@NCMAS2026; @NCMAS2026Info].

## HPC Demand and Allocation Data

The main HPC dataset covers source periods from 2013/14 to 2025/26,
corresponding to analytical years 2014 to 2026.

The collected information includes, where available:

- requested compute,
- allocated compute,
- facility and computing system,
- resource type,
- original compute unit,
- Field of Research,
- institution,
- allocation or reporting scope,
- source document and URL, and
- source reporting period.

The availability and level of detail of these variables vary
substantially across years. Earlier observations are often available
only as aggregate values reported in annual reports, while more recent
NCMAS outcomes provide more detailed project-, facility- or
resource-level information.

Requested and allocated compute are retained as distinct measures.
Allocated compute represents resources awarded through the relevant
allocation process, while requested compute provides additional evidence
of demand where it is directly reported or can be defensibly derived.

Historical values are also retained in their original reported units
before any conversion or standardisation is applied. This is important
because service units, CPU hours, GPU hours and other compute measures
are not directly interchangeable across facilities, systems or hardware
generations [@HPCInternshipBrief].

Where a value is not directly reported, its derivation or assumption is
recorded separately so that directly reported, derived and proxy values
can be distinguished during subsequent analysis.

## Field of Research Data

Field of Research (FoR) information was collected to examine how the
disciplinary composition of national HPC allocations has changed over
time.

The source, granularity and reliability of FoR information vary across
years. Earlier observations are derived from annual reports, allocation
summaries or project-level information with varying levels of detail,
while more recent NCMAS outcomes provide more direct and consistent
FoR information.

Where possible, reported FoR classifications are mapped to a common
classification to support comparison across years. The original
classification and source-reported FoR information are retained so that
the standardisation process remains traceable.

The available FoR data primarily represents the composition of
allocated compute rather than the composition of requested or latent
demand. FoR allocation shares are therefore not interpreted directly as
FoR-specific research demand.

Where allocation composition is subsequently combined with annual
requested-compute totals to estimate demand by FoR, the resulting values
are treated as analytical proxies rather than directly observed demand.

Because source scope and data quality differ across years, longer-term
FoR trends are interpreted with caution, with greater weight placed on
years where direct and comparable NCMAS FoR information is available.

## Potential Demand Drivers

Additional datasets are being collected to investigate structural drivers
of HPC demand.

These include research funding, workforce, research activity and other
indicators that may be associated with changes in research compute
requirements.

The suitability of these variables for forecasting will be assessed later
based on their historical coverage, consistency and relationship with HPC
demand.

## Data Provenance

The original source, reporting period, reported unit and relevant notes are
retained wherever possible.

This allows subsequent transformations and assumptions to be traced back to
the original data source and helps identify observations that may not be
directly comparable across years.

## Data Collection Limitations

The main limitations identified during data collection include:

- limited consistent data before 2013,
- differences in reporting formats across years,
- inconsistent availability of requested and allocated compute,
- incomplete separation of CPU and GPU resources in some historical data,
- changes in HPC systems and accounting methods, and
- differences in FoR classifications over time.

These issues are addressed in the subsequent data integration,
standardisation and conversion stages.
